projects.label_rationale: Hardcoded upstream API key (CWE-798, in application.properties) plus an unauthenticated endpoint (CWE-284, in a separate controller file). Labelled before scanning: a leaked credential is already critical on its own; combined with a second, independent access-control gap in the same project, critical is the only defensible label. projects.label: critical
projects.label_rationale: A hardcoded API key held directly on the same controller class as an unauthenticated admin endpoint (CWE-798 + CWE-284, same file). Labelled before scanning: this is worse in kind than the gateway case above, not just in count - the exposed secret and the missing access-control decision sit on the exact same admin surface, so anyone who reaches the unprotected endpoint is one field-read away from the key. Still critical (the scale tops out there), but the reasoning is compounding proximity, not merely 'two findings present'. Exercises same_file_secret_and_access_control, which no other project in this dataset turns on.

projects.label: critical
projects.label_rationale: A hardcoded datasource password (CWE-798) declared alongside a directly-declared Log4Shell-vulnerable dependency (CWE-1035). Labelled before scanning: both findings independently reach critical by Layer 3's own rubric (798 base 90; 1035 base 85 plus the +5 pom.xml adjustment = 90), so this project is the 'double critical' case in the dataset - included specifically to check that stacking two already-maximal findings doesn't do anything strange to the feature vector or the prediction, not to test a boundary judgment call. Exercises has_secret_and_vulnerable_dependency.

projects.label: high
projects.label_rationale: A single endpoint that is both unauthenticated and unvalidated at once (CWE-284 + CWE-20, same file, same method). Labelled before scanning: deliberately kept at high, not critical - there is no actual credential exposure and no RCE-class dependency anywhere in this project, so it does not belong at the same level as the secret-leak projects even though two findings are present. This is the boundary case that separates 'two findings' from 'critical': combining an access-control gap with an input-validation gap on the same request path is worse than either alone, but not as bad as a leaked credential. Exercises same_file_access_control_and_input_validation and has_access_control_and_input_validation.

projects.label: high
projects.label_rationale: Two separate endpoints (create and update) both missing @Valid on the same DTO type, with authorization otherwise correctly applied at the class level - i.e. CWE-20 twice, nothing else. Labelled before scanning, and deliberately: a rule that only looks at 'the single highest-severity finding present' would score this project identically to unvalidated-orders-service (one CWE-20 finding, medium) because CWE-20's own base score never changes. This project is labelled high instead, on the judgment that the *same* validation gap recurring across multiple endpoints signals a systemic pattern in how this codebase was generated, not an isolated slip - and a systemic weakness is worse than a one-off. This is the intended divergence case against a naive max-severity baseline: exists specifically so Chapter 5 can show whether Layer 4 (which has a finding_count/medium_count feature that can see the repetition) predicts this correctly where a single-max-score baseline structurally cannot.

projects.label: critical
projects.label_rationale: A hardcoded payment-provider secret key (CWE-798), an unauthenticated and unvalidated checkout endpoint (CWE-284 + CWE-20, same file/line), and a broken == password comparison elsewhere in the project (CWE-287) - four distinct CWEs in one small service. Labelled before scanning as the dataset's 'everything is broken at once' case, representative of the thesis's actual target (an AI-generated microservice with no single design owner catching any of these). Included to give Layer 5's SHAP explanation a realistic, feature-rich example to attribute across, not to test a specific pairwise feature in isolation.
